h1: Upskilling a brewery team with live online classes
title: Upskilling a Brewery Team Online | Craft Beer School
desc: How to train brewers, cellar staff and managers through live online classes: choosing topics, scheduling across time zones and applying lessons.
teaser: You cannot send the whole team to a brewing school. Live online classes bring the teacher to the brewhouse.
standfirst: Training that happens on the plant floor sticks. Here is how to plan live online learning for a brewery team, from picking topics to checking what changed.
sections: Why online works for brewery teams

A brewery rarely has spare staff. Sending a head brewer abroad for a fortnight stops the brewhouse. Online classes run at set hours, need no travel and let the learner go back to their own tanks, notes and data the next day. A live class beats a recorded video for this because the learner can ask a question about their own plant and hear the teacher's answer in the same hour.

The caveat is attention. A class watched on a phone in the middle of a shift teaches very little. Give the team a quiet room, a screen and protected time.
Start with the problem, not the course

List what is going wrong. Inconsistent batches, high losses, slow fermentations, packaging faults, poor records, a new product line? Match each to a skill and a person. A brewer who struggles with wort chemistry needs a different class from a manager who wants to read a cost report. Write the question you want answered by the end: for example, why does our lager finish with diacetyl, or why does our yield fall in summer?

Pick a few learners who can apply the lessons and share them. The best candidates are people who already ask why a step is done, who keep notes and who have the authority to change a procedure once they have seen the evidence. Training every person in a small team at once is often unnecessary. Train two and have them teach the rest.

Look for live teaching with a limited class size so questions are possible, weekly assignments that use the learner's own brewery, recordings for missed sessions and a certificate that shows completion. Check the teacher's background and the syllabus for the topics you need. Our Advanced Brewing Science course runs for 6 weeks on Saturdays and Sundays from 12:00 PM to 2:00 PM India Standard Time (UTC+5:30), with a maximum of 20 students per batch. Students join from their own time zone and recordings cover a missed class. Compare that to the working day in your country: at 12:00 PM in India, it is mid-morning in the Gulf, early morning in Europe and the middle of the night in much of the Americas, so weekend sessions suit some teams better than others.

The weekend schedule keeps classes out of the production week, but it takes personal time. Agree up front how you will recognise that, for example with time off in lieu, a training allowance or the company paying the course fee. Do not expect staff to learn after a 12 hour brew day. Sit down with the learner before the course and agree what they will do with the lessons afterwards, such as running a test on the plant or writing a short procedure.

Learning fades without use. After each class, ask the learner to do one small thing in the brewery: measure mash pH on the next brew, trace a loss with a mass balance, set up a fermentation log. Review it with them in a short meeting. Weekly assignments in a good course build this habit. See logging brewery data you will actually use for a record-keeping routine that makes the lessons visible.

Put the key lesson on one page and pin it where the team works. A mash pH target, a pitching sheet or a cleaning sequence on the wall is worth more than a certificate in a drawer. Share what was learned. A ten minute talk to the rest of the team on Monday spreads the value and gives the learner practice in explaining.

Define a measure before you start: batch consistency, yield, loss rate, shelf-life test results, customer complaints. Take a baseline before the course and compare after a few months. Do not expect a single class to transform results. Look for steady improvement in the thing you chose. If nothing changes, ask why. The topic may have been wrong, or the lessons may not have been applied.

For career growth, see learning to brew while working full time and working as a brewer abroad.
faqs: Can a live online class replace hands-on training?
It cannot replace practice on your own plant, but it teaches the science and decision-making behind the practice. The assignments push the learner to apply it at work.
What if our time zone does not suit 12:00 PM India time?
Classes are on weekends and recorded, so a missed live session can be watched later. Check the conversion for your location before enrolling.
How many people should I send?
Often two is enough. They can apply the lessons and teach the rest of the team.
